'''Larry F. Lemanski''' is 'Distinguished Research Professor' and Director of the '''Biomedical Institute for Regenerative Research''' ('''BIRR''') at [[East Texas A&M University]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.regenerativemedicinenow.com/texas-gets-1-6-million-regenerative-medicine-research|title=Texas A&M Gets $1.6 Million for Regenerative Medicine Research - Regenerative Medicine Now|date=30 May 2016|publisher=|access-date=12 October 2016|archive-date=13 October 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161013000206/http://www.regenerativemedicinenow.com/texas-gets-1-6-million-regenerative-medicine-research/|url-status=live}}</ref> He is also a Regents' Professor of the Texas A & M System, the highest level recognition for Texas A & M System's faculties.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.tamus.edu/texas-am-system-board-of-regents-recognize-exemplary-faculty-and-professionals/|title=Texas A&M System Board of Regents Recognize Exemplary Faculty and Professionals|date=Nov 10, 2016|website=The Texas A&M University System|accessdate=Aug 26, 2020}}</ref> He received a B.S. from [[University of Wisconsin, Platteville]] and then both M.S. and Ph.D. from [[Arizona State University]], [[Tempe, Arizona|Tempe]]. He was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], [[Philadelphia]] and worked there with Prof. Lee D. Peachey. He joined [[UCSF Medical Center]], [[San Francisco]] in 1975 as served as an Assistant Professor of Anatomy (1975–1977); he moved to [[University of Wisconsin, Madison]] and worked there as Assistant Professor (1977–1979) and Associate Professor (1979–1981). He was appointed as full Professor in 1981. He was Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs at [[East Texas A&M University]] during 2009–2012.<ref name="tamuc.edu">{{cite web|title=Larry F. Lemanski, Ph.D.|publisher=East Texas A&M University|url=http://faculty.etamu.edu/llemanski}}</ref>

==Research==
His main research interests concern a study of myofibrillogenesis and heart inductive processes in developing embryonic hearts at the cell and molecular levels. He has studied cardiac mutant axolotls, transgenic mice, and induced pluripotent adult stem cells. His goals have been to elucidate the sequence of events and mechanism(s) of myofibrillogenesis and to explain how inductive interactions direct heart differentiation at the cellular and gene levels. He is known for discovering unique and specific ribonucleic acids (RNAs) that have the capacity to promote cardiac myofibrillogenesis in non-muscle cells. He is pursuing the mechanism of this exciting and intriguing phenomenon and is exploring inducing heart muscle repair in hearts damaged from disease processes such as myocardial infarctions (heart attacks).
